inscrutable.literal: not able to be searched through
inscrutable.path: Latin scrutari meant to search thoroughly, originally to rummage through trash for something valuable. Inscrutable describes what cannot be searched out or understood.

insensate.path: From Latin sentire, to feel. Insensate describes what lacks feeling or sense entirely.

insensible.literal: not able to feel or perceive
insensible.path: Same sentire root as insensate. Insensible describes being unconscious or unaware, without sensation.

insidious.path: Latin insidiae meant an ambush, literally troops sitting in wait. Insidious describes harm that lies in wait, spreading gradually and hidden.

insinuate.path: Latin sinus meant a curve or fold, as in a toga or a bay. Insinuare meant to work one's way in through winding curves, giving insinuate its sense of hinting slyly or working in gradually.

insipid.path: Latin sapere meant to taste or to be wise. Insipid describes food or ideas that lack flavor or interest.

insist.path: Latin sistere meant to stand or take a stand. Insist means to stand firmly upon a demand or claim.

insolence.path: Latin solens meant customary, from solere, to be accustomed. Insolens originally meant unusual or unaccustomed, and came to describe arrogantly overstepping normal bounds, hence rude disrespect.

insolent.path: Same root as insolence. What was once merely unaccustomed or out of the ordinary came to mean rudely overstepping the bounds of respect.

insolvent.path: Latin solvere meant to loosen or release, extended to paying off a debt. Insolvent describes being unable to pay what is owed.

insouciance.path: French souci meant care or worry, from Latin sollicitare, to agitate. Insouciance is a casual, carefree lack of concern.

inspire.path: Latin spirare meant to breathe. Inspire originally meant a divine breath infused into a person, and came to mean stimulating creativity or motivation.

instance.path: Latin instare meant to stand close upon or press urgently. Instance came to mean a particular case that stands right before you, an example.

institute.path: Latin statuere meant to set up or establish, from stare, to stand. Institute means to set something in motion or establish it formally.

insufferable.path: Latin sufferre meant to carry from underneath, to endure. Insufferable describes what cannot be endured, especially unbearable arrogance.

insular.path: Latin insula meant island. Insular originally described island geography, then extended to a narrow, isolated outlook, as if cut off like an island.

insularity.path: The noun form of insular, from Latin insula, island, naming the narrowness of outlook that comes from being cut off.

insurgent.path: Latin surgere meant to rise. An insurgent is one who rises up in rebellion against established authority.

insurrection.path: From the same root as insurgent, Latin surgere, to rise. Insurrection names the violent uprising itself.

intelligible.path: Latin intelligere meant to perceive or understand, literally to choose or discern between things. Intelligible describes what can be clearly grasped.

intemperance.path: Latin temperare meant to mix in due proportion or restrain. Intemperance is the lack of that moderation, especially overindulgence in drink.

intend.path: Latin tendere meant to stretch. Intendere meant to direct one's attention toward a goal, giving intend its sense of planning or meaning to do something.

intensive.path: From the same tendere root as intend. Something intensive is stretched to its fullest degree, concentrated and thorough.

inter.path: Latin terra meant earth. Inter means to place a body into the earth, to bury.

interchangeable.path: Combines inter-, between, with change, ultimately from Latin cambire, to barter. Interchangeable things can be swapped for each other without difference.

interdict.path: Latin interdicere meant to forbid by formal proclamation, placing a decree between someone and an action. Interdict means to prohibit officially.

intermediary.path: From Latin medius, middle. An intermediary stands between two parties as a go-between.

interminable.path: Latin terminus meant a boundary or end point. Interminable describes something with no end in sight, endless and tedious.

intermittent.path: Latin mittere meant to send or release. Intermittere meant to pause or leave gaps between periods of activity, giving intermittent its sense of occurring at irregular intervals.

internecine.path: Latin internecinus meant utterly deadly, using inter- as an intensifier. Samuel Johnson's dictionary mistakenly read inter- as between, and that misreading fixed the modern sense of destruction mutual to both sides within a group.

interplay.path: A straightforward compound of inter-, between, and play. Interplay names the way things act and react upon each other.

interpolate.path: Latin interpolare originally meant to touch up or alter a text by inserting new material between the old lines, giving interpolate its modern sense of inserting something between existing parts.

interregnum.path: A direct Latin compound: an interregnum is the gap between one ruler's reign and the next.

intertwined.path: Combines inter-, between, with twine, from Old English twin, twisted thread. Intertwined things are twisted together closely.

intimate.path: Latin intimus meant innermost. Intimare meant to announce something as if from deep within, and the verb intimate kept a sense of hinting indirectly rather than stating outright.

intimation.path: The noun form of intimate, from Latin intimus, innermost, naming the indirect hint itself.

intractable.path: Latin trahere meant to drag or draw, and tractare meant to handle or manage. Intractable describes what cannot be handled or managed, hard to control or solve.

parts.meaning: to come to an agreement, settle

intransigent.path: Latin transigere meant to transact or settle a matter across differences. Intransigent describes someone who refuses to settle or compromise.

intrepid.path: Latin trepidus meant fearful or agitated. Intrepid describes someone who does not tremble in the face of danger, fearless.

intrigue.path: Latin tricae meant tangles or perplexing trifles. Intrigue originally meant to entangle or perplex, and the noun came to mean secret, entangling plots.

intrinsic.path: Latin intrinsecus described something located on the inward side. Intrinsic describes qualities belonging naturally to a thing's inner nature.

introspection.path: Latin specere meant to look. Introspection is the act of looking inward at one's own thoughts.

inundate.path: Latin unda meant wave. Inundate originally described a flood of water and extended to being overwhelmed by anything arriving in great quantity.

inure.path: The Old French phrase en ure meant in practice, from oeuvre, work. To inure someone to something means to bring them into habitual practice with it until they are accustomed or hardened.

inured.path: The adjective form of inure. Inured describes someone hardened by long exposure or habitual practice.

invasive.path: Latin vadere meant to go or walk. Invadere meant to go in aggressively, to attack. Invasive describes what intrudes or spreads aggressively into a space.

invective.path: Latin vehere meant to carry. Invehi meant to carry oneself against someone in words, to attack verbally. Invective is that abusive, attacking language.

inveigle.path: The word traces through Old French aveugler, to blind, ultimately Latin ab oculis, without eyes. To inveigle someone is to blind their judgment with flattery or deceit so as to persuade them.

investiture.path: Latin vestire meant to clothe. Investiture is the formal ceremony of clothing someone in the robes and symbols of office, conferring it upon them.

inveterate.path: Latin vetus meant old. Inveterate describes a habit so long-established and deeply aged into someone's character that it feels permanent.
